description_ru: Glacier ice: ice and semi-permanent snow; thickness largely unknown but in order of tens of metres; cirque glaciers, small mountain ice caps and valley glaciers; includes minor areas of loose morainal debris and nunataks (rock and colluvium-covered rock)
note: GSC Map 1609A Seymour Arm, BC (Fulton, Alley & Achard 1986), 1:250k, TM CM 116 (map margin), NAD27; colour scan; frame 118-120W 51-52N; description_ru holds the English legend text; swatches sampled at explicit positions (legend_from_points); glacier ice (pale blue stipple on white)fills calibrated on the map face (preview_tint_calib.py, PAPER seed) except O, Ca, Ch, Mm read inside labelled map polygons (calibration drifted 10-26 dE onto contour/linework mixtures)

description_ru: Organic deposits: peat, muck, minor sand, silt and tephra; up to 3 m thick; bogs and wetlands; only a few large deposits mapped

Colluvial apron materials: rubble and diamicton in the form of aprons of coalescing fans and cones; up to 10 m thick; rubble where the slope above is dominantly competent rock, diamicton where the source is morainal; locally includes alluvial deposits

Landslide materials: rubble and diamicton; topography hummocky to rolling; up to 100 m thick; dominantly blocks and rubble from local bedrock with rounded pebbles and finer material from morainal, alluvial and glaciofluvial sediments

Alluvial plain materials: sand, gravel, silt and minor organic sediment; up to 20 m thick; bar, channel and overbank deposits on floodplains, includes terraces, small fans and local organic deposits. Ac: dominantly channel deposits (sand and gravel), terraces common; Ao: dominantly overbank and deltaic deposits (sand and silt)
note: Ac and Ao share one tint (split legend box, told apart by labels only): merged unit Ac-Ao

description_ru: Alluvial fan materials: gravel, sand and diamicton; up to 40 m thick; fan or terraced-fan deposits; bouldery where gradients are steep

Alluvial complex materials: gravel, sand, rubble and diamicton; complex of intertonguing and overlapping alluvial deposits (Ac, Ao, Af) and colluvial fans and aprons (Ca); mapped in valleys where small, complexly interrelated units could not be subdivided

Lacustrine deposits: silt and fine grained sand with minor clay; up to 50 m thick; rhythmites and laminated bedding; deposited in lakes which formed behind glacier dams or in isostatically downwarped segments of valley; easily eroded and prone to slumping
Glaciofluvial terrace materials: gravel, sand and minor till; 2-40 m thick; terraces, locally with kettles; deposited between an ice tongue and confining slopes

Glaciofluvial materials, undulating: gravel, sand and minor till; 2-30 m thick. Gm: surface undulating to hummocky; G: underlies alluvial sediments in Columbia River valley; deposited on ice which later melted
note: Gm and G share one tint (split legend box): merged unit Gm-G

description_ru: Morainal blanket: till 2-5 m thick (sandy, silty and gravelly diamicton, matrix 40-80 % sand, 20-40 % silt, 5-20 % clay); includes isolated rock outcrops, patches of thicker till and minor other deposits
Morainal veneer: till less than 2 m thick; includes patches of bedrock and colluvium, pockets of thicker till and minor other deposits
Morainal blanket and veneer: area consisting of approximately equal proportions of morainal blanket and morainal veneer

Thick morainal deposits: sandy, silty and gravelly diamicton, in most places bouldery, with small areas of glaciofluvial sand and gravel; up to 18 m thick; low-relief (up to 5 m) hummocks and undulating terrain common

Rock, steep rock areas: crystalline metamorphic and igneous rocks, metasedimentary gneiss and schist, slate, phyllitic siltstone, greenstone; Precambrian to Paleozoic. Rock at the surface or under a discontinuous veneer or blanket of colluvium and till; steep slopes with minor lower slopes where colluvium and till thicken toward the toes
Rock, alpine rock areas: a complex of rock and rock blanketed by colluvium and till in an alpine mountain area characterized by aretes and cirques
